dietEvidence.body: The deep skull, robust jaws and spoon-shaped teeth are consistent with herbivory. Tooth replacement and jaw mechanics have been studied, but no gut contents are known; the plants eaten are inferred.

sizeNote: Length and mass are estimates from incomplete material, not measurements of a whole animal.
tagline: A common Morrison sauropod with a relatively short neck, a deep skull and spoon-shaped teeth. It is known from many individuals and growth stages.
summary: Camarasaurus supremus is a common Morrison Formation sauropod, known from multiple skulls and partial skeletons. It has a deep, relatively short skull with spoon-shaped teeth. Growth marks in dorsal ribs and cranial myology provide evidence for its growth and feeding, but no gut contents are known.

discovery.body: Named by Cope, 1877. The record is known from Morrison Formation, Colorado and Utah. Many partial and articulated skeletons, including juveniles.

fossilEvidence.title: Preserved material
fossilEvidence.body: Many partial and articulated skeletons, including juveniles.

fossilEvidence.title: Stratigraphic and geographic occurrence
fossilEvidence.body: Morrison Formation, Colorado and Utah records the species in the Late Jurassic. The numeric range used here is ≈155–145 Ma, an occurrence estimate rather than a direct date on every specimen.

fossilEvidence.title: Skull and growth series
fossilEvidence.body: Multiple skulls and partial skeletons are known. Dorsal-rib histology records growth marks; the sample shows variation in growth among individuals.

anatomy.title: Preserved anatomy
anatomy.body: The skull is large and deep, the neck is shorter than in diplodocids, and the limbs are robust.

behaviour.body: Behaviour is inferred from the skull and jaws: they are capable of cropping and processing vegetation, but habitual feeding height and social behaviour are reconstructed from anatomy and bonebed associations, not observed.

reconstruction.body: A licensed life reconstruction is assigned to this record and credited in Sources and credits. The species is known from many partial and articulated skeletons, including juveniles. The reconstruction is an artist's interpretation of appearance, not a direct observation from the fossil record; preserved integument, where present, is described in the anatomy section, and the soft-tissue outline is otherwise inferred.

confidenceNote: The skull and postcranium are well sampled. Growth and feeding are inferred from histology and biomechanics, and soft tissue is unknown.
